look_here_first: LOOK HERE FIRST · Slender UNARMED scrambling or clump-forming plant with often sharply TRIANGULAR / HASTATE leaves and three-angled green stems. Tiny WHITE (sometimes violet-tinged) five-lobed star flowers have roughly equal SEPARATE yellow anthers and occasionally a shiny green/white eye at the corolla base. Flower clusters usually 3–6. Fruits eventually BRIGHT RED (some local treatments describe dark red to almost black), but NO VERIFIED RIPE-FRUIT PHOTO IS PRESENT in this card. The chief look-alike is introduced bittersweet nightshade (S. dulcamara): usually purple swept-back flowers with more joined anthers and larger branching flower clusters; white dulcamara forms exist. Do not ID on berry color alone.

morphology_keys.family_pattern: Solanaceae/Solanum: alternate leaves, 5-parted rotate/stellate corollas, poricidal anthers, and berry fruits.
best_field_traits: Unarmed, thin-stemmed scrambling or ascending herb/subshrub; basal stems may be woody; stems often sharply three-angled / ridged.
Simple ALTERNATE leaves, often narrow triangular / hastate with basal pointed or rounded lobes, but leaf shape can vary greatly even on one plant.
WHITE or occasionally purple-tinted star corolla with five pointed lobes and shiny green or greenish-white corolla eye; the eye may require a macro.
Yellow anthers nearly equal and individually FREE rather than joined into a tube; FNA reports ~3.5–4 mm.
Small usually 3–6-flowered, unbranched or lightly forked cymes; fruit/flower pedicels insert into little sleeves on inflorescence axis.
Ripening to shiny RED berries (FNA ~10–15 mm), though local botanical descriptions include dark red/black fruit. Mature fruit NOT yet represented by a photo in gallery.
Cannot confirm anther pores, eye spots, or fully mature berry just from current Joey field photographs.
morphology_keys.comparison_training: KEY LOOK-ALIKE: S. dulcamara also scrambles, may have hastate leaves, green-eyed flowers and RED fruits. S. triquetrum has smaller 3–6 flower clusters, sharply angled stems, usually WHITE corolla and anthers free/individually distinct. S. dulcamara normally has larger 7–40-flowered branched clusters and reflexed PURPLE lobes (rare white forms). Black-berried American/European morelloids are generally herbs with different reproductive characters.
morphology_keys.habit: Semiwoody scrambling vine-like herb or subshrub, up to 2 m in FNA (Williamson County specimens often lower). Slender three-angled ridged unarmed shoots; may climb or thread through other shrubs and fences. Not a twining vine in the narrow structural sense.
morphology_keys.stems: Green often distinctly angled/ridged, unarmed (no prickles); at least two ridges may descend from leaf nodes. Woody towards base in older plants.
morphology_keys.leaves: Simple alternate triangular, deltate or hastate, sometimes mostly narrow linear and sometimes basally 2-lobed. Typical FNA ~1.8–5 cm long but variable; do NOT use leaf outline by itself.
morphology_keys.flowers: Usually small WHITE five-part stars, sometimes faint purple; green or green-white shiny eye at bases of corolla lobes (may be hard to see in these photos). Yellow anthers equal and FREE (not fused/cone), ~3.5–4 mm in FNA. Poricidal anthers may eventually open into slits, but terminal pores NOT resolved in current photos.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: Often unbranched or forked terminal/leaf-opposed 3–6-flowered cyme; pedicels inserted into sleeves and may droop with open flower. Compare introduced S. dulcamara's larger 7–40-flowered many-branched inflorescence.
morphology_keys.fruit: Shiny red berry usually ~1–1.5 cm in FNA, unlike black berries of Morelloid group; some central Texas reference material documents berries dark red to black and smaller. Color varies—obtain vouchered ripe local fruit photographs before teaching colors as absolute.
morphology_keys.habitat: Brush, thickets, fence edges, limestone slopes, moist places and woodland margins, Texas into northeastern Mexico. Retain existing Hays local/provisional range metadata unchanged.
morphology_keys.management: Field identification only. Nightshade leaves, unripe fruits and possibly ripe fruit can be poisonous; do not taste or recommend eating any berries from a photo identification.

field_terms.Hastate: Arrowhead-like leaf with two pointed spreading basal lobes.
field_terms.Anther: Yellow pollen-bearing structure on stamen; compare free versus connivent/cone-shaped anther positions.
field_terms.Connivent: Anthers brought close together or touching but not necessarily genetically or anatomically fused. Use term instead of incorrectly calling bittersweet nightshade anthers truly fused.
field_terms.Eye: Green or green-white shiny coloration near the center of the white/purple corolla at lobe bases.
field_terms.Pedicel sleeve: Small collar/sleeve at the point each flower stalk attaches to the shared flowering axis.
field_terms.Three-angled stem: Stem with three lengthwise ridges rather than round in cross-section.

crew_field_sequence: 1 · Trace the THIN SCRAMBLING stem and check no prickles. Feel/look for longitudinal angles/ridges without stripping or damaging a public plant.
2 · Examine several simple ALTERNATE leaves: are they sharply triangular or HASTATE, with two base lobes? Leaf shape can vary.
3 · Find an open flower: usually WHITE star with five lobes; inspect YELLOW anthers to see if each anther is separately visible rather than packed together as in bittersweet nightshade.
4 · Look for the green-white eye at the petal bases; do not assert it is present if your phone macro doesn't resolve it.
5 · Count the flowers on one stalk/cluster (typically 3–6), and photograph inflorescence branching + pedicel sleeves.
6 · If fruit is present, photograph a clearly RIPE fruit with calyx, leaf and shoot together. Red berry alone does not separate from introduced S. dulcamara.
7 · Compare against S. dulcamara: often PURPLE deeply reflexed corolla, closely arranged anthers, bigger branched clusters. Rare white-flowered dulcamara means color alone is never final.
8 · If only sterile leaves, record Solanum (Dulcamaroid clade) or compare triquetrum/dulcamara until flowers and fruit are available.

field_matrix.flower: Usually WHITE (sometimes purple-tinged); greenish eye possible; 5 free equal yellow anthers ~3.5–4 mm
field_matrix.leaf: Sharply triangular or HASTATE, some narrow or basally lobed
field_matrix.fruit: Shiny RED (local notes dark red to black); mature fruit photo missing
field_matrix.quick_rule: Thin ridged stem + triangular leaf + few white star flowers + individually distinct anthers.

field_matrix.flower: Usually PURPLE strongly reflexed lobes; sometimes WHITE; yellow anthers tightly connivent (clustered cone)
field_matrix.leaf: Variable broadly oval / heart-shaped to lobed
field_matrix.stems: Unarmed scrambling woody vines, usually rounder stems
field_matrix.quick_rule: Often purple reflexed star + cone-like tightly grouped yellow anthers + many-branched flower cluster; white exceptions exist.

field_matrix.flower: Very tiny WHITE star with short anthers ~0.8–1.5 mm
field_matrix.quick_rule: Short anthers and black ripe berries; generally not vine-like.

field_matrix.flower: Very short yellow anthers, five small white lobes
field_matrix.leaf: Oval, shallow wavy teeth; not characteristically triangular
field_matrix.quick_rule: Black-fruited Morelloid, unlike typical red-fruited triquetrum.

field_matrix.flower: Large YELLOW flower, conspicuously unequal anthers
field_matrix.quick_rule: Yellow flower + serious prickles = not triquetrum.

not_reliable_alone: One triangular leaf alone; both S. triquetrum and S. dulcamara have variable foliage.
WHITE vs PURPLE flower color alone; rare white-flowered S. dulcamara occurs.
One ripe RED berry alone; both scramblers can have red fruit.
A claim of flower-eye color or anther pore anatomy when current photo doesn't resolve it.
County-native certification inferred from a photo: retain existing range HOLD.

visual_comparison.title: Texas nightshade: TRIANGULAR leaves + FREE yellow anthers + tiny WHITE stars

visual_comparison.memory_rule: UNARMED angled scrambling stem, arrowhead leaves, few small WHITE flowers with FREE anthers; S. dulcamara usually has PURPLE bent-back stars and many flowers, but white exceptions exist.

items.label: 1 — Angled unarmed stems, triangular leaves, tiny white flowers
items.image_role: Scrambling unarmed stems, sharply triangular to hastate alternate leaves, small white flower cluster
items.creator: Joey Santore
items.caption: EXACT SPECIES from Joey Santore's documented iNaturalist observation 270192408. Small white flowers, slender unarmed green stems and pointed triangular/hastate leaves. CC BY-NC 4.0, noncommercial teaching use only, source photograph unmodified.
items.why_it_matters: LOOK FIRST for sharp triangular/hastate leaf outlines and slender three-angled unarmed shoots. Distinguish from broadly lobed S. dulcamara; however leaf variability means flowers and cluster are needed too.

items.label: 2 — Five white corolla lobes, separate yellow anthers, buds
items.image_role: White star-shaped flowers with separate yellow anthers, unopened buds, and sharply pointed basal leaf lobes
items.creator: Joey Santore
items.caption: EXACT SPECIES photographed by Joey Santore, iNaturalist photo 485889815. Open white star flowers with yellow, roughly equal anthers and unopened buds; flower size is small relative to the fingers in the photo. A shiny greenish floral eye can be subtle and is NOT securely resolved in this image. CC BY-NC 4.0.
items.why_it_matters: Flower color is usually white (sometimes violet-tinged) and the yellow anthers remain individually distinguishable, unlike the more tightly joined/conical anthers in bittersweet nightshade. Don't infer terminal pores without a high-magnification photo.

items.label: LOOK-ALIKE — bittersweet nightshade (DIFFERENT SPECIES)
items.image_role: Different species comparison: usually purple reflexed corolla and more clustered/connivent anthers
items.creator: Andrew Macumber
items.caption: THIS IS BITTERSWEET NIGHTSHADE (Solanum dulcamara), NOT TEXAS NIGHTSHADE. Usually PURPLE reflexed corolla, anthers held together in a narrow cone, commonly larger branched clusters (often 7–40 flowers). Rare WHITE-flowered S. dulcamara exists: compare anthers, leaves, stem angles and clusters rather than flower color alone.
items.why_it_matters: Both are unarmed scrambling Solanum that can make RED berries and flower centers with shiny GREEN/WHITE eye spots; purple/white color alone is not foolproof.
